note: Holds industry context, judgment dimensions, extra questions, evidence interpretation and job links. An industry does not change scores: `axis_emphasis` lists the axes that industry looks at more and is not part of the axis-level calculation. `scene` is a short introduction shown before Core screening and produces no score
reading_rule: An industry pack is not an industry trivia quiz. What it looks at is whether existing electrical and electronic experience can be recognized in, and connected to, that industry's problems. That is why each item has a `gloss` restating the judgment in general EE terms, and the test screen shows that line with the item. Not knowing an industry's vocabulary is never recorded as a poor fit

exploration.note: All eight industries can be explored in the results. At the start, the student picks up to two industries of interest, reads the chosen industries' scenes before Core screening, and in PRO one of them is asked in depth. Industries not chosen are compared lightly using the Core results. Industry packs are not put behind a subscription

demands: Process equipment needs small signals read out through noise
Any spread in device characteristics shows up straight away in yield, so measurements are repeated
High-voltage power supplies and precision measurement sit together inside one tool
Equipment downtime is written into contracts with customers
packs.scene: In semiconductor and display process equipment, EE graduates work on small-signal measurement, spread in device characteristics, high-voltage power supplies and equipment control. Setting circuit conditions and confirming them by measurement carries straight over.

demands: Much of the equipment cannot be reached for repair once it is deployed
Temperature, vibration and radiation are all weighed as design conditions
Standards and test procedures are fixed before the design starts
Quantities are small, so the reliability of each unit decides overall performance
packs.scene: In defense and aerospace, EE graduates work on circuits that run in harsh environments, RF and antennas, power systems and reliability testing. Taking standards as design conditions and backing them up with tests carries straight over.

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you take environmental conditions as design conditions?
judgement_dimensions.why: Temperature and vibration set circuit lifetime

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you read the standard's test items first?
judgement_dimensions.why: Without passing the tests, there is no delivery

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you get RF losses and matching right by design?
judgement_dimensions.why: Reflected power damages equipment

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you provide alternate paths for failures?
judgement_dimensions.why: Some places cannot be reached for repair

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you make the power system withstand sudden loads?
judgement_dimensions.why: Peak power is far above normal

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you back up lifetime with reliability testing?
judgement_dimensions.why: A single unit failing means mission failure

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you separate targets from noise through signal processing?
judgement_dimensions.why: Most of the received signal is of no use

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you take parts supply and discontinuation into the design?
judgement_dimensions.why: In long-lived equipment, parts disappear first

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you keep records that can be traced?
judgement_dimensions.why: Traceability of each judgment is the deliverable

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you treat EMC at the system level?
judgement_dimensions.why: Transmitters and receivers sit together in one system

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you trace the causes of failure back to the design stage?
judgement_dimensions.why: There is no room to repeat the same failure

judgement_dimensions.name: Do you keep communication links from dropping?
judgement_dimensions.why: Once a link drops, there may be no way to restore it

items.ask: Have you taken temperature and vibration conditions into a circuit design?
items.gloss: Building very cold or high-vibration environments into the design conditions

items.ask: Have you read a standard's test items first and written them down as design conditions?
items.gloss: Reading the tests to be passed in advance and building them into the design

items.ask: Have you set an RF structure to reduce reflected power?
items.gloss: Changing a structure so reflected power would not damage the circuit

items.ask: Have you provided an alternate path so it keeps running if one side fails?
items.gloss: Building a backup path so it keeps working if one side fails

items.ask: Have you set up a power supply to withstand loads that jump suddenly?
items.gloss: Designing a power supply to cope with sudden jumps in power demand

items.ask: Have you measured under harsh conditions whether it would last over long use?
items.gloss: Running an accelerated test under harsh conditions to see what long use would do

items.ask: Have you separated what to keep from what to discard in a received signal?
items.gloss: Picking out only the needed signal from noise

items.ask: Have you chosen components with long-term availability in mind?
items.gloss: Choosing parts after checking they could be obtained for a long time

items.ask: Have you kept records so it was possible to trace which decisions were made and why?
items.gloss: Keeping records so the reasons for a decision could be looked up later

items.ask: Have you set the margin for a communication link that cannot be restored once it drops?
items.gloss: Leaving a generous signal margin so a communication link would not drop
